title: How do we find the angle at O?
description: Two lines are parallel, and a bent path joins them. New lines through the bends, parallel to the first two, give alternate angles. A split angle is taken apart and put back together, and a closing check adds the pieces.
teaching_notes: One idea: a line drawn through a bend, parallel to the given lines, turns an angle that cannot be read into alternate angles that can. Watch for students who add forty, ninety six and fifty two.

video_script.why: The child splits an angle and uses alternate angles, as in the solved example, with new lines drawn through the bends of a path.
video_script.substitution: the book's own figure: LM parallel to PQ, a path M, N, O, P between them, angle at M is forty degrees, angle MNO is ninety six degrees, angle OPQ is fifty two degrees
video_script.anchor: two parallel lines LM and PQ with a bent path M, N, O, P between them, the angle at M marked 40°, angle MNO marked 96° and angle OPQ marked 52°
video_script.payoff_line: Two new parallel lines split one hard angle into two known angles

final_answer.spoken: angle N O P is one hundred and eight degrees

maths_rules: draw a line through N and a line through O, both parallel to LM and PQ
the line through N makes 40 with NM, an alternate angle of the angle at M
the rest of the angle at N is 96 - 40 = 56
the angle between ON and the line through O is also 56, an alternate angle
the angle between OP and the line through O is 52, an alternate angle of the angle at P
video_script.design: One figure for the whole video. The two new lines are dashed. Each pair of alternate angles takes one colour, and the angle at O shows its two smaller angles.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about a bent path between two lines.
<bookmark mark='par'/>The lines L M and P Q are parallel.
<bookmark mark='path'/>The path goes from M to N, then O, then P.
<bookmark mark='m'/>At M, the angle between M L and M N is forty degrees.
<bookmark mark='n'/>At N, the angle between N M and N O is ninety six degrees.
<bookmark mark='p'/>At P, the angle between P O and P Q is fifty two degrees.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Find the angle N O P.

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

narration: <bookmark mark='alt'/>Two angles between parallel lines, on opposite sides of a transversal, are called alternate angles.
<bookmark mark='eq'/>Alternate angles are equal.
<bookmark mark='new'/>We can draw a new line parallel to the two lines. It gives us more alternate angles.

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, L M is parallel to P Q.
<bookmark mark='angles'/>At M the angle is forty degrees. At N it is ninety six degrees. At P it is fifty two degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the angle N O P.

narration: <bookmark mark='alt'/>Step two, look at N. The new line makes forty degrees with N M, as an alternate angle of the angle at M.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>The rest of the ninety six degrees at N is ninety six take away forty. That is fifty six degrees.
<bookmark mark='book'/>This is the same way as the example in your book.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: at O, the angle between ON and the new line is 56°; the angle between OP and the new line is 52°

beats.colours: each pair of alternate angles has its own colour
narration: <bookmark mark='fifty'/>Step three, look at O. The two new lines are parallel.
<bookmark mark='alt'/>The angle between O N and the line through O is also fifty six degrees. It is an alternate angle.
<bookmark mark='pp'/>The angle between O P and that line is fifty two degrees. It is an alternate angle of the angle at P.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: angle NOP is made of these two angles, 56° + 52° = 108°

narration: <bookmark mark='join'/>Step four, the angle N O P is made of these two angles.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Fifty six and fifty two make one hundred and eight.

marks.sum: 40 + 56 = 96 is written beside the angle at N

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step five is the check. Forty and fifty six make ninety six, the angle at N.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Two new parallel lines split one hard angle into two known angles.
